name: Rafael Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining, Rafael. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers or government, and what you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I sell flats and houses for Keyline, a newer agency in the city that does most things through an app and charges lower fees. My day is viewings across four or five postcodes, valuations in the afternoon, and offers coming in on my phone while I'm driving between them. I use an AI assistant every day for drafting emails, summarising surveys and prepping my valuation notes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the negotiation, the moment when a seller's holding out for ten grand more and you find the deal both sides can live with. What wears me out is the hours, because Keyline promises viewings until eight at night. My girlfriend Ama is a freelance graphic designer, and between us we're doing fine, with about three months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was bigger than the tools, but the tools are still useful. I'd keep posting the odd tip on LinkedIn about how I use AI for valuation prep. People at Keyline already think I'm the AI guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep a small edge and nothing else changes. I'd be slightly faster than the agents who don't use AI, which shows up as one or two extra sales a quarter. That's nice, but it's not life-changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep using the tools, and push for more valuations, since I can prep them in half the time. I'd also start saving for a deposit with Ama, maybe four hundred a month between us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, actually. Bit of a letdown, because I like new things, but my job and money would feel solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries in this picture that have nothing to do with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hours, and the market. Keyline grew fast on cheap fees, and if the market slows they might cut agents. But I'm decent and I'm cheap to keep, so I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ama say about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be relieved. Design work got squeezed by the image tools already, so a plateau means her clients stay. She'd probably say I was too excited about it all along.

Nothing **life-changing** happens to my job or pay.

Save about **£400 a month** with Ama towards a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say agents who use AI will replace agents who don't, which is a bit of a cliché but true. I'd offer to run a session at Keyline on how I use it. I'd be loud about it, because being the person who knows it is protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Keyline is exactly the kind of firm that cuts first, because the whole model is fewer people and cheaper fees. Booking, chasing, answering buyers, all that goes to software. I think they'd keep the best negotiators and give each of us twice the patch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person who sets up the AI tools for the team in the first few months. I'd ask for a small pay rise or a title for it. And I'd start a side thing, maybe helping small independent agents set up the same tools for a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but also a bit excited. I think I'd come out of this one alright, but I'd be watching my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ama in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what worries me more, honestly. Writing and design tasks go to AI here, and she's freelance with no notice period. If her income halves, we're on my commission alone, and that's not great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd start a side business while doing longer hours at Keyline. When?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saturday mornings and the odd evening. I'd keep it small, two or three agencies, a few hundred each. If it worked I'd think about doing it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest change of our lives and anyone pretending otherwise is kidding themselves. I'd probably post a long thread about what it means for property. People would read it, because they'd all be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job as it is today is gone by 2028. Valuations, negotiating, the paperwork, it's all thinking work, and the AI would be better at it than me. The one thing left is standing in a kitchen with a nervous buyer, and that lasts until the robots, maybe 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd go all in on the in-person side: offering hosted viewings and open days for other agencies' listings, paid per viewing. I'd keep our three months of savings untouched and cut eating out. With Ama, I'd ask if she wants to pivot with me, because her design work would be going too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I'd be busy, and busy helps. It would hit both of us at once, which is the bit that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deposit fund would turn into a survival fund. Then the car, which I need for viewings, so maybe a cheaper one. We'd stop the trip to Ghana to see my grandmother, which would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd be fine being busy, but it keeps you up. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. In the day I'd be making plans and feel okay. At two in the morning I'd be doing sums on my phone about how long three months lasts with two incomes gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if you use it. I'd tell people at Keyline to stop arguing about whether it's real and start planning. I'd be a bit preachy about it, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years lets me build something before 2031 instead of scrambling after. My guess is the money in property moves to owning and fixing up homes, not selling them. Hands-on renovation work lasts until about 2034 here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Keyline for two or three years and use AI to sell more than ever while it's still my edge. Ama and I would buy a run-down flat with the deposit fund, renovate it on weekends, and rent it out. I'd do a short course on renovation and project management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but energised. It feels like a race I can actually run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't a renovation flat a big risk with three months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. We'd need a mortgage, and if both our incomes drop before it's rented, we're stuck. I'd only do it with a fixed rate and a cheap enough place that rent covers it with room to spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ama think of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd do the design side, picking finishes and staging photos, which she's good at. She's more careful than me, so she'd make me run the numbers three times. That's probably healthy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and the smart ones will be fine. I'd keep running training at Keyline and writing about it. I'd probably sound quite relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd still expect to stop being an agent by my late thirties. But ten years means I can sell, save and build up a couple of rental flats first. That's a different life from the two-year picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in sales, use the extra commission to build the deposit, and buy our first flat within three years. Then a second one to renovate around 2030. I'd also keep the side business helping small agencies with AI, as long as it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a bit of watchfulness. I'd want to make sure I don't get lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousins about careers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade and learn AI, both. My cousin Kwame wants to be an agent like me, and I'd tell him to do it for a few years but have a hands-on skill too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything in this picture worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ama's work, still. And the idea that everyone has the same plan to buy property, which pushes prices up. If everybody runs to bricks and mortar, flats get too expensive for people like me to buy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Ama and I would both be hit in the same year. What would help is some kind of income floor for a year while people switch, and banks being willing to lend to people mid-career change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people would still trust an AI with the biggest purchase of their life. I think a lot of buyers would want a human in the room just to blame if it goes wrong. That might be my job for longer than anyone thinks.

headlineQuote: A lot of buyers would want a human in the room just to blame if it goes wrong.
portrait: A **27-year-old** sales negotiator at Keyline, a low-fee app-based agency in the city.
Uses AI **every day** and is seen at work as the office's AI person.
Lives with his girlfriend Ama, a **freelance designer** whose work is even more exposed.
Moves from **calm** in the plateau to alarmed when AGI comes in two years.
Plans to shift from selling homes to **owning and renovating** them as time allows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both household incomes would be hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: A **year-long income floor** for people switching careers.
Banks willing to **lend mid-career** to people changing jobs.
